title: BBC Paid £130M for Lonely Planet. Why Sell at a Loss?
description:
The day after Christmas 1972, a young couple arrived in Sydney with just 27 cents left. A year later, at their kitchen table, they stapled together their first travel guide. Thirty-four years later, the buyer of that publisher was the BBC's commercial arm.

This episode goes in order: how a battered car and a kitchen table became Lonely Planet; the BBC buying in twice, and paying the original price for the last quarter; Parliament calling it "the most egregious example"; the reasons written down in the official review; the 2013 sale, and how the loss of "nearly 80 million pounds" was worked out.

Where the narration uses secondhand accounts or estimated figures, it says where they come from and how they were calculated. The illustrations are AI-generated; people who are alive, or who died less than seventy years ago, are not drawn, only objects, hands or unrelated passers-by.

Information as of 2026-10-31

t001.text: You may have leafed through a thick backpacker guidebook.

t002.text: To buy the company that made it, the BBC paid about 130 million pounds, all told.

t003.text: The day after Christmas 1972, a young couple reached Sydney with just 27 cents left.

t004.text: A year on, they stapled their first guide in their kitchen.

t005.text: Born like that, worth over 100 million pounds?

t006.text: And the founders' last quarter: what price did the BBC pay for it?

t007.text: And the BBC's own website later made a decision.

t008.text: This file lays out six years of that money, item by item.

t009.text: What did those 130 million pounds buy in the end?

t010.text: Earlier that year, the Wheelers bought a battered car and left London,

t011.text: planning to drive east as far as they could go.

t012.text: Afghanistan, India, Thailand, all the way to Australia.

t013.text: In Sydney, people kept asking: where did you go, and how?

t014.text: So they put the answers in a book.

t015.text: In 1973, at that kitchen table from the start: the two wrote and stapled, one copy at a time.

t016.text: Its title meant crossing Asia on the cheap; it ran under 100 pages.

t017.text: Guess how many this home-stapled booklet sold in its first week.

t019.text: When I first read it, I thought it had an extra zero.

t020.text: In 1975 they published another, all about Southeast Asia.

t021.text: Backpackers later gave it a nickname. What?

t023.text: Wheeler said wherever the book went, people followed.

t024.text: Guess how big that stapled little book grew.

t025.text: By 2007, it had over 500 titles and sold over 6.5 million copies a year.

t026.text: Its website drew 4.3 million visitors a month.

t027.text: I think a kitchen-table publisher this big was bound to attract a buyer.

t028.text: On October 1st that year, someone came knocking.

t029.text: It was the BBC's commercial arm, and it bought three quarters of the company.

t031.text: A later BBC press release spelled it out: 88.1 million pounds.

t032.text: The other quarter stayed with the Wheelers.

t033.text: So what was the BBC after?

t034.text: Its chief executive said the deal fit its strategy:

t035.text: growing its content brands online, and expanding in Australia and America.

t037.text: But if you're British, your first thought is probably: what about my licence fee?

t038.text: The BBC later stressed no public money was used.

t039.text: Its watchdog, the BBC Trust, hesitated and set four conditions,

t040.text: and wanted proof the deal would make BBC programmes and brands worth more.

t041.text: On day one, the Guardian and the Financial Times both slammed it.

t042.text: A Guardian editorial called it "blundering commercialism".

t043.text: To be fair, the Guardian itself noted in the piece that it's a rival too.

t044.text: Two years later, it was Parliament attacking.

t045.text: In April 2009, the Commons Culture, Media and Sport Committee issued a report.

t046.text: It said the balance had tipped too far to the arm's unchecked growth.

t047.text: Worse, the accounts were turning ugly.

t048.text: In the year to the end of March 2009, it lost 3.2 million pounds.

t049.text: In September came a follow-up report. Its words?

t050.text: Of the arm's moves into fields the BBC barely worked in, buying it was the most egregious example.

t051.text: The report also said the Trust, meant to keep watch, seemed arrogant.

t052.text: Honestly, called out like that by Parliament, I'd want to crawl into a hole.

t053.text: That month, a London city magazine's founder said it lost money hand over fist,

t054.text: the BBC kept pouring in millions. Why not force them to sell it?

t055.text: At year's end the Trust ruled: no more such deals, barring exceptional circumstances.

t056.text: If you were a BBC executive then, what would you do? Sell, or hang on?

t057.text: They hung on. And the business really seemed to turn around.

t058.text: In February 2011, papers reported it back in profit, earning 1.9 million pounds.

t059.text: Non-print revenue went from 9 percent of the total to 22 percent.

t060.text: In February 2011, the Wheelers pulled a card from their contract.

t061.text: This card was a put option: the right to make the buyer take the rest.

t062.text: Remember the question from the start? What price for that last quarter?

t064.text: For that last quarter, the BBC paid 42.17 million pounds.

t065.text: As the seller, that's likely your best contract ever, right?

t066.text: The later official review put it bluntly: this put option was badly structured.

t067.text: The reason: results fell well short, yet the contract took nothing off the price.

t068.text: The chairman then said the put option kept the Wheelers' know-how in the firm for three and a half years.

t070.text: That's the roughly 130 million pounds from the start.

t071.text: That May, Australian publishing trade media reported up to 70 jobs would go in Melbourne,

t072.text: and much of the web work would move to London.

t073.text: And the Wheelers left the company they had built themselves.

t074.text: But to make money online, this company needed more than itself.

t075.text: The question: who did it rely on?

t076.text: The Trust had the BBC do the review itself, led by a non-executive director with outside advisers.

t077.text: It said the web business was to plug into the BBC's international site and sell ads together.

t078.text: Remember the start? What did the BBC's own website do?

t080.text: And then? Guess what it did.

t081.text: Delayed, it decided to make its own travel section.

t082.text: The report said these delays made decent ad money harder to earn.

t083.text: Pay a fortune for a travel firm, then build your own travel section? Odd, no?

t084.text: Like buying a coffee maker, yet buying coffee downstairs daily.

t085.text: Take America: travel books sold in 2012 were down 19 percent on the year before.

t088.text: It was slow online too; the report said it might have taken the TripAdvisor path,

t089.text: or ridden the home-sharing wave that followed.

t090.text: Last trip abroad, did you find restaurants in a book, or in reviews on your phone?

t091.text: The report traced the problem to the day of purchase: the plan assumed a 30 percent operating margin.

t092.text: Too optimistic, it said; the buyer seemed swept up in the deal, not working out how fast book sales could fall.

t093.text: So, was it all the BBC's fault?

t094.text: Beyond its control, it said: a shock Aussie dollar surge, the crash,

t096.text: By March 2013, the BBC gave up.

t097.text: On March 19, the BBC announced it was selling the whole company, for 75 million Australian dollars.

t099.text: And not all at once: 60 million Australian dollars up front, 15 million a year later.

t100.text: When it sold, its website drew over 120 million people a year,

t101.text: and its app had been downloaded over 11 million times.

t102.text: The buyer was a company based in Nashville, Tennessee, in the US,

t103.text: and its main shareholder: a Kentucky-born landowner made rich by cheap cigarettes.

t104.text: The backpackers' bible, ending up with a tobacco tycoon. Who saw that coming?

t105.text: The official reason: it no longer fit a plan centered on the BBC's own brands.

t106.text: So how much did the BBC lose?

t107.text: AFP and the Guardian wrote then: nearly 80 million pounds.

t108.text: Simple math: the 130 million from the start, minus that sale price.

t109.text: But that money wasn't all lost on the day of the sale.

t110.text: The Guardian wrote that over six years, the BBC had already written down 67 million pounds.

t111.text: So its book value slid from that opening 130 million all the way to 63 million.

t112.text: On the day it actually sold, the loss on the books was only about 12 million.

t114.text: But what if you count it another way?

t115.text: The official review said about 20 million pounds more went in during those years.

t116.text: Estimating from the report's own figures, all in, the loss is close to 100 million pounds.

t117.text: The Trust admitted that day: this wasn't a good commercial investment.

t118.text: And the people who sold to the BBC, how did they see the deal?

t119.text: That September, the AP interviewed Tony Wheeler.

t120.text: He said: no question, we sold at the perfect moment.

t121.text: Remember the Aussie dollar the report named? Wheeler said they sold just as it took off.

t122.text: That's honest, and a little cruel.

t123.text: He also said the BBC missed one thing: in Italian-language guidebooks, it was the biggest seller.

t124.text: Two months later, the BBC spoke up again. The Trust's vice-chair said:

t125.text: mistakes were made in buying and running it.

t126.text: Remember that old car driving east from London?

t127.text: Two years on, at a Bali writers' festival, he was blunter with Reuters:

t128.text: A total disaster. They bought this car, but didn't fill it up or hit the gas.

t129.text: They got in and just asked: what do we do? Let's drive slowly.

t131.text: At the end of 2020, it was sold again, price undisclosed.

t132.text: Today it has about 130 full-time staff; the year the BBC sold, it had 400.

t133.text: The books still come out, in 33 languages, with over 150 million copies printed.

t134.text: Next time in a bookshop, think of the ledger behind it.

t135.text: Back to the opening question: less than half the money came back. Why?

t136.text: Remember that review? Its answer: valued too high, changed too slowly, hit by bad timing.

t137.text: Guidebook abroad, or only your phone? Let me know below.

t138.text: This channel sticks to the record. Subscribe to open the files with me.
